title: Joint-Space Empowerment as a Theory of Dexterous Motor Coordination
claim: A learned low-dimensional action manifold, framed as a noisy communication channel from latent actions to body motion, enables coordinated control of an overactuated system.
layout: 3 panels: two image panels and manifold on top, pipeline below, left-to-right
description: The top row has two black-background renderings of a musculoskeletal hand and forearm. The left one, in a red frame, is labeled 'actuation' and shows red tendon and muscle lines over the bones. The right one, in a green frame, is labeled 'joint motion' and shows the skeleton in motion with ghosted fingers. To the right, panel b shows a blue curved surface labeled 'precoder manifold'. An orange dot marks the latent action on it. Red axes are labeled action 1, action 2 and action M, and the states s and s' are marked on the surface. Panel c is a left-to-right pipeline built from circles, trapezoids and a cylinder. The latent action z_t goes into the precoder g_θ, then to the action a_t, then to the dynamics P(s_{t+1}|s_t,a_t), then to the next state s_{t+1}. The joint-space decoder h then produces the joint velocities y_{t+1}. A bracket labels the middle stages as an adaptable noisy communication channel between a sender and a receiver. Colors match across panels: orange for latent action, red for action, green for joint velocities.

abstract: Searching for effective policies in high-dimensional action spaces is notoriously challenging. This difficulty is compounded in overactuated musculoskeletal systems, where multiple muscles span each joint, and individual muscles actuate multiple joints. Although this redundancy complicates naive policy search, it also implies that effective control can be captured by a low-dimensional action manifold. To identify such a manifold, we introduce joint-space empowerment (JSE) , a novel information-theoretic principle that quantifies how much control an agent has over its body. We use JSE to discover high-empowerment action manifolds, and demonstrate that manipulation policies learned on these manifolds show significantly enhanced dexterity, sample efficiency and improved generalization. These results suggest a general principle for motor coordination in high-dimensional, overactuated systems, with implications for both biological motor control and embodied artificial agents.
